\phantomsection\label{\detokenize{index::doc}}


\sphinxAtStartPar
The code is separated into 5 parts: the 4 parts as described in the Architecture
overview of the specification (chapter 5.1) and the hardware drivers.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This actuator supports both the reader side and the user side of the protocol. The class
that implements the reader side is the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader.Reader}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Reader}}}}}, and the user side is
implemented by the {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UserDevice}}}}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Both {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader.Reader}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Reader}}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UserDevice}}}}} have a similar structure.
They both have a parameter transport\_protocol (of type {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.defines:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.defines.TransportProtocol}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TransportProtocol}}}}})
which indicates which transport protocol to use (NFC or BLE/UWB). After instantiating
the class, the {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.transaction_initiation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transaction\_initiation()}}}}}
or {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader.Reader.transaction_initiation}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{transaction\_initiation()}}}}} method
is used to set up the connection to a device.
This method blocks until the connection is established.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UserDevice}}}}} and
{\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.reader.Reader}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Reader}}}}} can now be used in one of
two ways: using the handle functions for an easy to use approach, or the command/response
methods for more control.


\chapter{Approach 1 (handle)}
\label{\detokenize{index:approach-1-handle}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach uses the attributes set during instantation, and the ones received from
commands, to make the actuator easier to use. Start by using the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.start_new_session}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_new\_session()}}}}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start\_new\_session()}}
to start a session. All data received will be stored in this session.
The {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{UserDevice}}}}} now needs to wait
for a command. This is done with the
{\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.wait_for_command}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{wait\_for\_command()}}}}} method,
which returns a {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.apdu:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.apdu.Command}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Command}}}}} to pass to a handle method.
Now, use the methods that start with ‘handle’ to handle the commands:

\item[] {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.handle_select}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{handle\_select()}}}}}
\item[] {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.handle_auth0}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{handle\_auth0()}}}}}

\item[] {\hyperref[\detokenize{aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device:aliro_actuator.access_protocol.user_device.UserDevice.handle_control_flow}]{\sphinxcrossref{\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{handle\_control\_flow()}}}}}

\chapter{Approach 2 (command/response)}
\label{\detokenize{index:approach-2-command-response}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
This approach gives more control to the programmer. The methods that start with
‘command’/’response’ require a value for every piece of data they will send. The data
received will also need to be manually processed by the programmer (unlike Approach 1,
there is no session to save received data).
Note that Approach 1 also uses these ‘command’/’response’ methods, so you can use the
Approach 1 methods as an example.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Class for creating and parsing APDU messages.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the parse\_command/response functions to parse the received commands/responses.
Use the create\_\textless{}cmd\textgreater{}\_command/response to create new command/responses.
The as\_bytes attribute of these commands/responses gives a bytestring which can be send.

\sphinxAtStartPar
has the following attributes:
support\_extended\_length\_apdu: bool (set to true to support extended length APDU’s, see 8.3 Aliro spec)

(length is calculated using the data and does not need to be specified)
